newsitem.title: USA: U.S. plans to appoint coordinator for Tibet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plans to appoint coordinator for Tibet.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in a letter to a Congressional panel on Wednesday she planned to appoint a special coordinator to oversee U.S. policy toward Tibet, a move that may anger China.

Albright, who is travelling in Asia, said in a letter read to the panel that the coordinator would deal exclusively with Tibetan issues but that this did not constitute U.S. recognition of Tibet as an independent state. The coordinator would be appointed by Nov.1.

"A central objective of this position will be to promote substantive dialogue between the Government of the People's Republic of China and the Dalai Lama or his representatives," Albright said in the letter.

President Bill Clinton met exiled Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama at the White House in April and urged China to open a dialogue with him. China criticised the meeting, saying the U.S. was interfering with Chinese internal affairs.

Albright said the U.S. coordinator would "vigorously promote the U.S. policy of seeking to protect the unique religious, cultural and linguistic heritage of Tibet, and pressing for improved respect of human rights."

The appointment of a special coordinator is a compromise with the joint House-Senate panel, which is drawing up a bill on restructuring the U.S. State Department. The bill had included a clause for the appointment of a special envoy, a provision Albright strongly opposed.

Albright was concerned that establishing a formal position for a Tibetan envoy would further strain relations with China, which has long claimed sovereignty over Tibet. She would prefer to appoint a special coordinator, which would be less than the full rank of ambassador.
Albright said the coordinator would maintain close contact with the religious and cultural leader of the Tibetan people, including travel to Tibet.

However, since the United States regarded Tibet as a part of China, these contacts would not constitute any form of diplomatic recognition of the Tibetan government-in-exile or promote the independence or secession of Tibet from China.
North Carolina Republican, Sen. Jesse Helms, said provisions for the special envoy would be dropped from the bill. "I think this is a good arrangement," he told the conference committee.

Barbara Larkin, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Legislative Affairs, told the panel that Albright would appoint the co-ordinator before Nov. 1 and that she would discuss the appointment with Congress.
